Mental health

Anxiety

What anxiety is, when it becomes a problem, how it is assessed and which treatments work.

Medical review Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Need help now? In Spain, 024 is free and open 24 hours; in an emergency call 112. Elsewhere, contact your local helpline or emergency services. This text is for general information: it cannot diagnose and does not replace seeing a professional. Where to get help →

What it is

Anxiety is a normal reaction to a threat or an uncertain situation. It prepares the body to act: the heart speeds up, breathing quickens, muscles tense and attention focuses on danger. In the right measure it is useful: it helps us study before an exam or cross the road carefully.

It becomes a problem when it is out of proportion, lasts a long time or limits daily life. Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health problems: they affect around 4% of the world's population in any given year, according to the World Health Organization.

Most common forms

  • Generalised anxiety: excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, almost every day, for months.
  • Panic disorder: sudden attacks of intense fear with palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness or a sense of impending death, and fear of further attacks.
  • Agoraphobia: avoiding places or situations from which it would be hard to escape or get help.
  • Social anxiety: intense fear of being watched, judged or embarrassed.
  • Specific phobias: of animals, heights, blood, flying or other particular things.

What it is not

Feeling nervous before an interview or worrying about a real problem is not a disorder. Nor is it "weakness" or lack of willpower. And it is not always psychological: an overactive thyroid, some heart rhythm problems, too much caffeine, certain medicines or alcohol withdrawal can produce similar symptoms. That is why a medical assessment is worthwhile, especially if symptoms are new.

How it is assessed

The family doctor or psychology professional asks about the symptoms, how long they have lasted, what triggers them and how much they interfere. Brief questionnaires such as the GAD-7 are often used; they guide but do not diagnose on their own. Physical causes are ruled out when appropriate, and substance use and mood are explored, because anxiety and depression often occur together.

Which interventions are studied

  • Cognitive behavioural therapy: the psychological treatment with the strongest support. It involves understanding the anxiety cycle, reviewing catastrophic thoughts and, above all, gradual exposure to what is feared instead of avoiding it.
  • Guided self-help using books or online programmes based on cognitive behavioural therapy, useful in mild to moderate cases.
  • Medication: some antidepressants (SSRIs and SNRIs) are effective for several anxiety disorders. Benzodiazepines bring quick relief but are recommended only for short periods because of the risk of tolerance and dependence.
  • Physical exercise, regular sleep and cutting down on alcohol and caffeine help as a complement.

How to seek help

If anxiety stops you doing things you want or need to do, a good first step is your family doctor, who can assess, treat and refer you to psychology or mental health services. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call 024 (in Spain) or your local crisis line.

How to support someone

Listen without downplaying it ("it's not a big deal") and without feeding avoidance. Encouraging the person to face their fears step by step and to seek professional help does more good than doing things for them or reassuring them over and over.

Myths to avoid

  • "A panic attack can cause a heart attack or make you go mad". It is very unpleasant, but it does not damage a healthy heart or cause madness.
  • "It's best to avoid what scares you". It brings short-term relief; in the long run it maintains and spreads the fear.
  • "If you take medication you'll need it forever". Many people stop it gradually under supervision.
